title: Research Analyst
blurb: Economy, industry, company, valuation and technicals, plus the SEBI rules for publishing research. Fifteen chapters, deeply worked.

units.title: Introduction to the research analyst profession
units.overview: Who a research analyst is and what the role demands.
facts: Research analyst
A research analyst studies securities, companies or markets and publishes recommendations, targets or opinions that investors may rely on.
A person who writes a report recommending a share with a target price.
A research analyst executes trades for clients.
Buy-side and sell-side
Sell-side analysts work for brokers and publish research for clients; buy-side analysts work for fund managers and research for their own investment decisions.
An analyst at a mutual fund researches stocks only for the fund's use.
Buy-side analysts publish reports for the public.
Objectivity and independence
Research must be independent, based on facts and free of undue influence from the subject company or trading desks.
An analyst resists pressure to change a rating after the company objects.
An analyst may change a rating at the request of the subject company.

units.title: Introduction to the securities market
units.overview: A rapid overview of the market that analysts operate in.
focus: Primary and secondary markets, participants and regulators.
facts: Securities market regulators
SEBI regulates the securities market, RBI the money market and banks, and exchanges oversee their members.
A research report on listed shares is subject to the capital-market regulator.
The RBI regulates research analysts.
Market segments
The securities market has equity, debt, derivatives and commodity segments, each with its own instruments and participants.
An analyst may cover shares, bonds and futures contracts.
Securities markets have only an equity segment.
Listing and disclosure
Listed companies must make continuous disclosures under the SEBI listing regulations, which are the primary source of information for analysts.
A company files its quarterly results and announces material events on the exchange.
Listed companies need not disclose results to the public.

units.title: Terminology in equity and debt markets
units.overview: Key terms the analyst must use correctly.
facts: Market capitalisation
Market capitalisation is share price multiplied by shares outstanding, and classifies companies as large, mid or small cap.
A company with 50 crore shares at ₹200 has a value of ₹10,000 crore.
Market capitalisation is the company's total assets.
Yield to maturity
Yield to maturity is the annualised return on a bond if held to maturity and coupons are reinvested at the same rate.
A bond priced below face value has a yield above its coupon.
Yield to maturity equals the coupon rate always.
Face value and issue price
Face value is the nominal value of a security, while the issue price is what investors pay at the time of issue, which may differ.
A share with face value ₹10 is issued at ₹250.
Issue price is always equal to face value.
Credit spread
Credit spread is the extra yield on a risky bond over a risk-free government bond of similar maturity, compensating for credit risk.
A corporate bond yields 2% more than a similar G-sec.
Credit spread is the difference between bid and ask.

units.title: Fundamentals of research
units.overview: The framework for doing research: approaches, sources and a disciplined process.
facts: Top-down approach
The top-down approach starts with the economy, then selects industries and finally companies.
An analyst first judges growth, then picks sectors, then picks stocks.
A top-down approach starts with a single stock.
Bottom-up approach
The bottom-up approach starts with individual company analysis and gives less weight to macro and sector views.
An analyst picks strong businesses irrespective of sector or economy.
A bottom-up approach starts with the global economy.
Fundamental analysis
Fundamental analysis estimates a security's intrinsic value from economic, industry and company factors and compares it with market price.
An analyst studies earnings and cash flow to judge fair value.
Fundamental analysis relies only on price charts.
Technical analysis
Technical analysis studies price and volume history to forecast future price moves, assuming patterns repeat.
An analyst studies charts and indicators rather than financial statements.
Technical analysis studies a company's balance sheet.
Qualitative analysis
Qualitative analysis assesses non-numerical factors such as management quality, brand, competitive position and governance.
An analyst evaluates the integrity and track record of the management.
Qualitative analysis uses only financial ratios.
Quantitative analysis
Quantitative analysis uses numerical data and models, such as ratios, forecasts and statistics, to evaluate securities.
An analyst builds a forecast model of revenue and profits.
Quantitative analysis ignores numbers.
Intrinsic value
Intrinsic value is the estimated true worth of a security based on fundamentals, which may differ from market price.
A stock priced at ₹80 is estimated to be worth ₹110.
Intrinsic value is today's market price.
Primary and secondary data
Primary data is collected directly by the analyst, such as management interviews and channel checks; secondary data is taken from existing sources like filings.
An analyst visits a plant to gather information first-hand.
Annual reports are primary data collected by the analyst.
Research process
The research process involves defining the objective, collecting data, analysing, valuing, forming a view, writing and monitoring.
An analyst follows steps from data gathering to publishing and updating.
The research process ends with the first report.
Margin of safety
Margin of safety is the gap between intrinsic value and the price paid, providing a cushion against errors in estimation.
An analyst buys only when price is well below estimated value.
A margin of safety means paying more than intrinsic value.

units.title: Economic analysis
units.overview: How the economy drives sectors and stocks: growth, inflation, policy and the cycle.
focus: GDP, inflation, fiscal and monetary policy.
visuals: Rate at which banks borrow from RBI
Share of deposits banks keep with RBI
Share of deposits banks hold in liquid assets
Buying or selling G-secs to adjust liquidity
facts: GDP
Gross Domestic Product is the total value of goods and services produced within a country in a period, a measure of economic activity.
A country's total output for the year rises 6.5%.
GDP is the total government spending.
Inflation
Inflation is the sustained rise in the general price level, measured in India by the Consumer Price Index and the Wholesale Price Index.
The general price level rises 5% compared with last year.
Inflation is a fall in the general price level.
CPI and WPI
CPI measures changes in retail prices faced by consumers, while WPI measures wholesale prices of goods. The RBI targets CPI inflation.
The policy target is based on retail prices.
The RBI targets WPI inflation.
Fiscal deficit
The fiscal deficit is government expenditure minus revenue (excluding borrowings), showing how much the government must borrow.
The government spends ₹50 lakh crore against receipts of ₹45 lakh crore.
The fiscal deficit equals the trade deficit.
Current account deficit
The current account deficit arises when a country's imports of goods, services and transfers exceed its exports.
India buys more from the world than it sells.
A current account deficit means the government has a budget deficit.
Monetary policy
Monetary policy is the central bank's use of interest rates and liquidity tools to manage inflation and growth.
The RBI raises the repo rate to control prices.
Monetary policy is set by the finance ministry.
Fiscal policy
Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxation and spending to influence the economy.
The government cuts taxes to stimulate demand.
Fiscal policy is set by the central bank.
Business cycle
The business cycle consists of expansion, peak, contraction and trough, with different sectors outperforming in each phase.
An economy moves from recovery to boom and then slowdown.
The economy grows in a straight line without cycles.
Leading indicators
Leading indicators such as new orders and PMI change before the economy turns and help forecast direction.
A rise in new orders signals growth ahead.
Leading indicators change after the economy turns.
PMI
The Purchasing Managers' Index surveys business activity; a reading above 50 indicates expansion and below 50 contraction.
A manufacturing PMI of 56 shows expansion.
A PMI below 50 shows expansion.
IIP
The Index of Industrial Production tracks changes in the volume of production in mining, manufacturing and electricity.
A monthly number shows industrial output rising 4%.
IIP measures retail inflation.
Exchange rate impact
A weaker rupee helps exporters' revenues but raises import costs, affecting sectors differently.
IT exporters gain when the rupee depreciates.
A weaker rupee hurts all companies equally.
Interest rate impact
Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and discount rates, which usually pressure valuations and rate-sensitive sectors.
A rate hike hurts real estate and auto stocks.
Higher interest rates always lift all share prices.

units.title: Industry analysis
units.overview: Industries have their own economics. This chapter equips analysts to assess structure, competition and lifecycle.
facts: Porter's five forces
Porter's model assesses industry attractiveness by competitive rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers and suppliers.
An analyst evaluates how easy it is for rivals to enter and compete.
Porter's model measures a company's profit margin.
Barriers to entry
Barriers to entry, such as capital needs, regulation, brands and scale, protect existing firms from new competitors.
A telecom sector needs spectrum and heavy capital.
High barriers to entry make an industry easy to enter.
Industry life cycle
Industries pass through start-up, growth, maturity and decline stages, with different growth rates and risks.
A new technology sector is in rapid growth with high uncertainty.
All industries remain in the growth stage.
Cyclical industry
A cyclical industry's earnings rise and fall sharply with the economic cycle, as in steel, autos and capital goods.
A steel company's profits swing with the economy.
Cyclical industries have stable earnings in all conditions.
Defensive industry
A defensive industry sells essentials with stable demand, such as FMCG, utilities and pharma, and holds up better in downturns.
A toothpaste maker's sales remain steady in a recession.
Defensive industries are the most sensitive to the economic cycle.
Industry concentration
Concentration measures how much of the market is held by a few firms; the Herfindahl-Hirschman index is one such measure.
Three firms hold 80% of the market, indicating concentration.
A concentrated industry has many equal small players.
Cost structure
Operating leverage depends on fixed versus variable costs; high fixed costs magnify profit swings as volume changes.
A firm with high fixed costs sees profits jump sharply when sales rise.
Fixed costs change in proportion to sales.
Substitute threat
Substitutes limit the prices an industry can charge, as customers can switch to alternatives.
Rising bus fares push travellers to trains.
Substitutes have no effect on pricing.
Regulation and policy
Government policy, taxes and regulation can change industry profitability, such as price controls in pharma or spectrum charges in telecom.
A price cap reduces margins in a regulated industry.
Regulation never affects industry profits.
PESTLE analysis
PESTLE reviews political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors that affect an industry.
An analyst lists the policy, tech and legal drivers for a sector.
PESTLE is a ratio of price to earnings.
Market share
Market share is a company's sales as a percentage of the industry total and shows competitive strength over time.
A firm's share rises from 20% to 25% over three years.
Market share is the same as profit margin.
Capacity utilisation
Capacity utilisation shows the share of installed capacity actually used; low utilisation signals weak demand or excess capacity.
A cement industry running at 60% capacity has spare supply.
High capacity utilisation always signals weak demand.
SWOT analysis
SWOT lists a company's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats to summarise its position.
An analyst lists internal strengths and external risks in one table.
SWOT is a method of calculating cost of capital.

units.title: Company analysis: business and governance
units.overview: Before the numbers, understand the business and the people running it.
facts: Business model
A business model describes how a company creates, delivers and captures value, and what drives its revenue and costs.
An analyst maps how a company earns each rupee of revenue.
A business model is the company's balance sheet.
Economic moat
An economic moat is a durable competitive advantage, such as brand, network effect, cost advantage or switching cost, protecting long-term profits.
A strong brand allows a company to charge premium prices for years.
An economic moat is a short-lived advantage.
Management quality
Management quality is judged by track record, capital allocation, transparency, integrity and alignment with shareholders.
An analyst reviews how past acquisitions performed and whether guidance was met.
Management quality is irrelevant if the numbers are good.
Corporate governance
Corporate governance is the system of rules and practices by which a company is directed and controlled, protecting shareholders' interests.
Independent directors, audit committee and transparent disclosures.
Corporate governance is only about paying dividends.
Board independence
Independent directors on the board and its committees provide oversight free from management and promoter influence.
A board has independent directors chairing the audit committee.
Independent directors are promoter relatives.
Related-party transactions
Dealings between a company and its promoters or their entities may favour insiders, so they require disclosure and approval.
A company buys goods from an entity owned by the promoter's family.
Related-party transactions need no disclosure.
Promoter pledge
Pledging of promoter shares to raise loans is a red flag, because a price fall can lead to forced sale and loss of control.
Promoters have pledged a large share of their stake.
A high promoter pledge is a positive sign.
Auditor red flags
Frequent changes of auditors, qualified audit opinions and delays in results can signal accounting or governance problems.
An auditor resigns mid-year citing lack of information.
A qualified opinion is a sign of clean accounts.
Capital allocation
Capital allocation is how management uses cash: reinvesting, acquiring, repaying debt or returning cash to shareholders.
A company uses free cash flow to buy back shares and cut debt.
Capital allocation means issuing more debt.
ESG
Environmental, social and governance factors affect long-term risk and returns and are increasingly part of research.
An analyst reviews a company's emissions and labour practices.
ESG factors have no financial relevance.
Disclosure quality
Transparent, timely and consistent disclosure builds trust; poor or selective disclosure is a warning sign.
A company explains its results and risks in detail.
Disclosures are only a legal formality.

units.title: Company analysis: financial analysis
units.overview: The core of the analyst's craft: reading financial statements and ratios. Expect many calculation questions.
focus: Profitability, liquidity, leverage and efficiency ratios.
visuals: ROE = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
facts: Income statement
The income statement reports revenue, expenses and profit over a period, showing how sales become net profit.
An analyst studies a company's sales and profit for the year.
The income statement shows assets and liabilities.
Balance sheet
The balance sheet shows a company's assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a point in time; assets equal liabilities plus equity.
A snapshot of what the company owns and owes on 31 March.
The balance sheet shows cash flows for a year.
Cash flow statement
The cash flow statement reports cash from operating, investing and financing activities, showing how cash moved.
An analyst checks whether profits convert into cash.
The cash flow statement lists only dividends.
EBITDA
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a proxy for operating performance before capital structure and non-cash charges.
A firm's operating profit before depreciation and financing cost.
EBITDA is the net profit after tax.
Net profit margin
Net profit margin is net profit divided by revenue, showing how much of each rupee of sales becomes profit.
Profit of ₹10 crore on revenue of ₹100 crore is a 10% margin.
Net profit margin is profit divided by equity.
Return on equity
ROE is net profit divided by shareholders' equity, showing the return earned on owners' funds.
A firm earns ₹20 crore on equity of ₹100 crore.
ROE is net profit divided by total assets.
Return on capital employed
ROCE is EBIT divided by capital employed (equity plus debt), measuring returns on all capital in the business.
EBIT of ₹30 crore on capital employed of ₹150 crore gives 20%.
ROCE uses only shareholders' equity in the denominator.
Current ratio
The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, showing short-term liquidity.
A firm with current assets of ₹200 crore and current liabilities of ₹100 crore has a ratio of 2.
The current ratio measures long-term debt.
Quick ratio
The quick ratio excludes inventory from current assets and divides by current liabilities, a stricter test of liquidity.
An analyst removes stock from current assets before testing liquidity.
The quick ratio includes inventory.
Debt-to-equity ratio
The debt-to-equity ratio is total debt divided by shareholders' equity and shows financial leverage.
A company with ₹300 crore debt and ₹200 crore equity has a ratio of 1.5.
Debt-to-equity is profit divided by equity.
Interest coverage ratio
Interest coverage is EBIT divided by interest expense, showing how comfortably a company can pay interest.
EBIT of ₹60 crore against interest of ₹20 crore gives 3 times.
Interest coverage is debt divided by equity.
Asset turnover
Asset turnover is revenue divided by total assets and shows how efficiently assets generate sales.
A firm generates ₹2 of sales for every ₹1 of assets.
Asset turnover measures profit per share.
Inventory days
Inventory days is average inventory divided by cost of sales times 365, showing how long stock sits before being sold.
A firm holds stock for 60 days on average.
Inventory days measure how long customers take to pay.
Receivable days
Receivable days measure the average time taken to collect payment from customers.
A firm waits 75 days to collect its dues.
Receivable days measure the time taken to pay suppliers.
Cash conversion cycle
The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days, showing how long cash is tied up in operations.
A shorter cycle means cash returns to the business faster.
A longer cash conversion cycle is always better.
Free cash flow
Free cash flow is cash from operations minus capital expenditure, representing cash available to investors after sustaining the business.
A company generates ₹100 crore from operations and spends ₹40 crore on capex.
Free cash flow equals net profit.
Operating leverage
Operating leverage reflects the share of fixed costs in total costs; higher fixed costs magnify the effect of sales changes on profit.
A small rise in sales produces a large rise in profit for a firm with big fixed costs.
Operating leverage measures debt in the capital structure.
Quality of earnings
Earnings are high quality when they are backed by cash flows, repeatable and not inflated by one-offs or aggressive accounting.
A company's profit is consistently supported by operating cash flow.
Earnings quality is judged by the size of one-off gains.
Common-size statements
Common-size statements express every line as a percentage of a base such as revenue, making comparison across firms and years easier.
An analyst expresses each cost as a share of sales.
Common-size statements show absolute amounts.
Ind AS
Indian Accounting Standards converge with international standards and govern how listed Indian companies prepare financial statements.
A listed company follows standards aligned with IFRS.
Ind AS applies only to banks.
Earnings per share
EPS equals profit after tax available to equity shareholders divided by the weighted average number of shares.
Profit of ₹100 crore on 20 crore shares is ₹5 per share.
EPS is the dividend per share.
Working capital
Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities and shows the funds tied up in day-to-day operations.
A firm's short-term assets exceed its short-term obligations by ₹50 crore.
Working capital is long-term debt.

units.title: Corporate actions
units.overview: Dividends, bonuses, splits, rights, buybacks, mergers and open offers, and what each means for shareholders and valuation.
facts: Ex-dividend date
The ex-dividend date is the date from which a share trades without the right to the declared dividend; buyers on or after it do not receive it.
An investor buys on the ex-date and does not get the dividend.
Buyers on the ex-date receive the dividend.
Record date
The record date is the date on which a shareholder must be on the company's register to be eligible for a corporate benefit.
Only holders on a specified date are entitled to the dividend.
The record date is the date the dividend is paid.
Bonus issue
A bonus issue gives existing shareholders extra shares free of cost in a ratio, capitalising reserves, with the price adjusting.
A company gives 1 free share for every 2 held.
A bonus issue raises fresh funds for the company.
Stock split
A stock split reduces the face value and increases the number of shares in the same ratio, leaving market capitalisation unchanged.
A ₹10 face value share splits into five shares of ₹2 each.
A stock split reduces the company's equity capital.
Rights issue
A rights issue offers existing shareholders the right to subscribe to new shares in proportion to their holding, usually at a discount.
A company offers 1 new share for every 5 held at ₹150.
A rights issue is offered to new investors first.
Share buyback
A buyback is the repurchase of a company's own shares, reducing the share count and returning cash to shareholders, through tender offer or open market.
A company buys back its shares at a premium to market price.
A buyback increases the number of shares.
Merger
A merger combines two companies into one, with the shareholders of the merged company receiving shares in the surviving company under a swap ratio.
One company absorbs another and issues its shares to the other's holders.
A merger splits a company into two.
Demerger
A demerger splits a business into two or more entities, and shareholders receive shares in the new entity in a given ratio.
A conglomerate separates its financial arm into a new listed company.
A demerger combines two companies.
Open offer
An open offer requires an acquirer who crosses the 25% trigger or acquires control to offer to buy shares from public shareholders under SEBI takeover rules.
An acquirer who takes 26% must make an offer to other shareholders.
An open offer is made only to the promoters.
Delisting
Delisting is the removal of a company's securities from an exchange, either voluntarily or compulsorily.
A company buys out public shareholders and its shares stop trading.
Delisting means a company issues new shares.
Dividend yield
Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the share price and shows income return.
A share at ₹200 paying ₹6 yields 3%.
Dividend yield is profit per share.
Dividend payout ratio
The dividend payout ratio is the share of profit paid as dividends; the rest is retained for growth.
A company pays ₹4 of ₹10 EPS, a 40% payout.
The payout ratio is dividend divided by price.

units.title: Valuation principles
units.overview: Turning analysis into a price. Intrinsic and relative valuation methods, their assumptions and limits.
visuals: Value today = Next year's dividend ÷ (Required return − Growth rate)
Required return = Risk-free rate + Beta × (Market return − Risk-free rate)
facts: Discounted cash flow
DCF values a business as the present value of its expected future free cash flows, discounted at the required rate of return.
An analyst projects cash flows for ten years and discounts them to today.
DCF values a business by multiplying earnings by a ratio.
Free cash flow to firm
FCFF is the cash available to all capital providers after operating costs and investment, discounted at WACC to value the firm.
An analyst computes cash available to both lenders and shareholders.
FCFF is cash available only to shareholders.
Free cash flow to equity
FCFE is the cash available to shareholders after debt payments and reinvestment, discounted at the cost of equity.
An analyst values the equity using cash left after servicing debt.
FCFE is discounted at WACC.
WACC
The weighted average cost of capital blends the cost of equity and after-tax cost of debt in proportion to their weights, and is the discount rate for FCFF.
A firm funded 60% by equity at 12% and 40% by debt at 8% (after tax 6%) has a blended cost.
WACC uses only the cost of equity.
Cost of equity (CAPM)
CAPM estimates the cost of equity as the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.
With a risk-free rate of 6%, beta of 1.2 and market return of 12%, the required return is 13.2%.
CAPM estimates cost of debt.
Terminal value
Terminal value represents the value of cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period, often a large share of total DCF value.
An analyst assumes cash flows grow steadily forever after year ten.
Terminal value is ignored in DCF.
Dividend discount model
The DDM values a share as the present value of expected dividends; in the Gordon model, value = D1 ÷ (r − g).
A share paying ₹5 next year with growth 5% and required return 15% is valued at ₹50.
The DDM values shares using book value.
Price-to-earnings multiple
P/E divides price by earnings per share and is a relative valuation tool, compared with peers and history.
A stock at 25 times earnings is compared with sector peers.
P/E is price divided by book value.
Price-to-book multiple
P/B compares market price with book value per share, widely used for banks and asset-heavy firms.
A bank trading at 2.5 times book value.
P/B is used mainly for software firms.
EV/EBITDA
EV/EBITDA compares enterprise value with operating earnings before depreciation, neutral to capital structure, useful for comparing leveraged firms.
A firm with EV of ₹5,000 crore and EBITDA of ₹500 crore trades at 10 times.
EV/EBITDA ignores debt entirely.
Enterprise value
Enterprise value is market capitalisation plus debt minus cash, the price of the whole business.
A company with market cap ₹1,000 crore, debt ₹300 crore and cash ₹100 crore has EV of ₹1,200 crore.
Enterprise value equals market capitalisation.
PEG ratio
The PEG ratio divides the P/E by the expected earnings growth rate, adjusting the multiple for growth.
A P/E of 30 with growth of 15% gives a PEG of 2.
The PEG ratio is the P/E multiplied by growth.
Relative valuation
Relative valuation values a security by comparing multiples with those of similar companies or its own history.
An analyst compares a bank's P/B with peers.
Relative valuation requires projecting cash flows.
Sum-of-the-parts
Sum-of-the-parts values each business unit separately and adds them, useful for conglomerates.
An analyst values a group's three divisions separately and sums them.
Sum-of-the-parts uses only a single multiple.
Sensitivity analysis
Sensitivity analysis shows how the valuation changes when key assumptions such as growth or discount rate are altered.
An analyst shows value at different discount rates.
Sensitivity analysis fixes all assumptions.
Intrinsic versus market value
A recommendation compares intrinsic value with market price: buy if undervalued, sell if overvalued, after allowing a margin of safety.
An analyst recommends buying when the market price is below fair value.
Market value always equals intrinsic value.
Equity risk premium
The equity risk premium is the extra return investors require from equities over the risk-free rate.
Investors demand 6% more than government bonds for equity risk.
The equity risk premium equals the risk-free rate.
Book value
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding, from the balance sheet.
Equity of ₹500 crore on 10 crore shares is ₹50 per share.
Book value per share is the market price.
Cyclically adjusted earnings
For cyclical firms, valuation based on peak or trough earnings misleads, so analysts use average or normalised earnings.
An analyst uses mid-cycle earnings for a steel company.
Peak earnings are always the right base for cyclical stocks.

units.title: Fundamental analysis of commodities
units.overview: Commodities are valued by supply, demand and cost of carry rather than earnings.
facts: Commodity price drivers
Commodity prices are driven by supply, demand, inventories, weather, policy and the currency.
A poor monsoon cuts crop output and raises prices.
Commodity prices depend only on company earnings.
Stock-to-use ratio
The stock-to-use ratio compares closing stocks with consumption; low levels signal tightness and price pressure.
Inventories fall to a few weeks of consumption and prices rise.
A low stock-to-use ratio signals oversupply.
Seasonality
Agricultural commodities show seasonal price patterns tied to harvests and demand cycles.
Prices of a crop tend to fall after harvest.
Seasonality is unimportant for agricultural prices.
Cost of carry in commodities
The cost of carry includes storage, insurance and financing costs, and links futures prices to spot prices.
A commodity future trades above spot by the cost of storing it.
Cost of carry has no effect on futures prices.
Gold drivers
Gold prices are influenced by real interest rates, the US dollar, central bank buying, inflation expectations and risk sentiment.
Gold rises when real interest rates fall.
Gold falls whenever inflation expectations rise.
Crude oil drivers
Crude oil prices are driven by OPEC+ decisions, global demand, inventories and geopolitical events.
Production cuts by major producers raise prices.
Crude oil prices are unaffected by supply decisions.
Currency link
Many commodities are priced in dollars, so a weaker rupee raises their domestic prices, other things equal.
Imported edible oil gets costlier when the rupee falls.
The rupee has no effect on domestic commodity prices.
Futures curve
The futures curve plots prices across expiries; contango signals plentiful supply and backwardation signals tightness.
Near-month prices exceed far-month prices when supply is short.
Backwardation means plentiful supply.

units.title: Fundamentals of risk and return
units.overview: The portfolio theory behind research: expected return, volatility, correlation and CAPM.
visuals: Sharpe = (Portfolio return − Risk-free return) ÷ Standard deviation
facts: Expected return
Expected return is the probability-weighted average of possible returns of an investment.
An asset has a 50% chance of 20% and a 50% chance of 0%, giving 10%.
Expected return is the highest possible return.
Variance and standard deviation
Variance measures the dispersion of returns around the mean; standard deviation is its square root and the common measure of volatility.
A stock's returns swing widely around its average.
Standard deviation is the average return.
Correlation
Correlation measures how two assets move together, from −1 to +1; lower correlation gives greater diversification benefit.
Two assets with correlation near zero reduce portfolio volatility when combined.
A correlation of +1 gives the best diversification.
Systematic risk and beta
Systematic risk is market-wide and measured by beta; it cannot be diversified away.
A stock with beta 1.3 amplifies market moves.
Beta measures company-specific risk.
CAPM
The Capital Asset Pricing Model states that expected return equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium.
A stock's required return is built from risk-free rate and market risk premium.
CAPM says return depends on total risk.
Security market line
The security market line plots expected return against beta; securities above it are undervalued.
A stock offering more return than CAPM predicts lies above the line.
The security market line plots return against standard deviation.
Sharpe ratio
The Sharpe ratio is excess return over the risk-free rate divided by standard deviation, measuring return per unit of total risk.
A fund earns 14% with risk-free 6% and standard deviation 16%, giving 0.5.
The Sharpe ratio uses beta as the risk measure.
Treynor ratio
The Treynor ratio is excess return divided by beta, measuring return per unit of systematic risk.
A portfolio's excess return is divided by its beta.
The Treynor ratio uses standard deviation.
Jensen's alpha
Jensen's alpha is the return in excess of the CAPM-predicted return, showing a manager's value addition.
A fund earns 2% more than CAPM predicts.
A negative alpha indicates outperformance.
Efficient frontier
The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios offering the highest expected return for each level of risk.
A set of optimal portfolios that cannot be improved on both return and risk.
Every portfolio lies on the efficient frontier.
Risk-free rate
The risk-free rate is the return on an investment with no default risk, such as the government security yield.
A ten-year G-sec yield is used as the base rate.
The risk-free rate is the rate on corporate bonds.
Diversification benefit
Combining imperfectly correlated assets reduces portfolio risk without a proportional fall in return.
Adding gold to an equity portfolio smooths overall volatility.
Diversification increases portfolio risk.
Downside risk
Downside risk measures the chance and size of losses below a target, as in semi-deviation or maximum drawdown.
An investor tracks how far a fund fell from its peak.
Downside risk counts only positive returns.
Maximum drawdown

facts: Report structure

A report opens with the rating and the key reasons.
A report need not state a recommendation.
Recommendation and rating
A rating such as buy, hold or sell must be defined, with the basis stated, and applied consistently.
A report defines buy as an expected return above 15% over twelve months.

Target price
A target price is the analyst's estimate of a security's price over a stated horizon, backed by a valuation method and assumptions.
An analyst sets ₹500 with a twelve-month horizon using a P/E method.
A target price needs no supporting valuation.
Risk disclosure in reports
A report should state the key risks to its thesis, so readers understand what could go wrong.
A report lists regulatory changes and input costs as risks.
Reports should hide risks to appear persuasive.
Clarity and objectivity
Clear language, supported claims and balanced treatment of positives and negatives make a report credible.
A report cites sources for each figure.
A good report uses exaggerated claims.
Reasonable basis
Every recommendation must have a reasonable basis supported by research and data, not mere speculation or rumour.
An analyst bases her call on filings and a valuation model.
A recommendation can rest on market rumours.
Timeliness and updates
Reports should be updated when material events occur and should state the date and data cut-off.
An analyst revises the target after the quarterly results.
A report never needs revision after publishing.
Data sources and accuracy
Sources should be reliable and cited, and numbers cross-checked for accuracy.
An analyst verifies figures with filings.

units.title: Legal and regulatory environment
units.overview: SEBI's Research Analyst Regulations: registration, conduct, disclosures, trading restrictions, records and penalties. Many exact-rule questions.
facts: SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations, 2014
These regulations require research analysts and research entities to register with SEBI and follow rules on qualification, conduct, disclosure and records.
A person who publishes recommendations for the public must hold SEBI registration.

Registration and qualification
An individual research analyst must hold the prescribed qualification and the NISM research analyst certification and meet other norms.
A candidate cleared the NISM examination and holds the specified degree.

Research entity
A research entity is a person such as a broker or company that issues research reports and must be registered; it can employ analysts.
A brokerage house publishing reports must be a registered entity.
A research entity is an individual client.
Disclosure of conflicts
A research analyst must disclose any financial interest, ownership or relationship with the subject company in the report.
A report states that the analyst holds shares of the company.
Analysts need not disclose holdings.
Trading restriction around reports
A research analyst must not deal in securities for 30 days before and 5 days after publishing a report on them.
An analyst cannot trade a stock for a period around her report.
An analyst may trade the stock in the hour before publication.
Assured returns prohibited
A research analyst must not provide, or claim to provide, assured or guaranteed returns.
A report says 'This stock will double in a year for sure.'
An analyst may guarantee returns for large clients.
Record keeping
Research analysts must maintain records of research reports, recommendations and the basis for them for at least five years.
An analyst retains her models and reports on file for five years.
Records must be kept for only six months.
Compliance officer
Registered research entities must appoint a compliance officer who monitors compliance and reports to SEBI as required.
A firm assigns a person to monitor adherence to regulations.
A compliance officer is optional.
Chinese wall
A Chinese wall is a set of information barriers that separates research from other business such as investment banking and trading to prevent misuse of sensitive information.
The research desk is kept apart from the banking desk.
A Chinese wall allows free flow of information.
Front running
Front running is trading ahead of a client's order or an upcoming report to profit from its expected impact, and is prohibited.
An analyst buys shares before releasing a strong buy report.
Front running is allowed if disclosed at a later date.
Insider information
An analyst must not use or share unpublished price-sensitive information, which is an offence under insider trading rules.
An analyst learns of a merger from a source and trades on it.
Using inside information is permitted for research analysts.
Client agreement
An analyst providing services to clients must sign an agreement stating the services, fees and terms, and give disclosures.
A client signs a document setting out the services and fees.
A written agreement is unnecessary.
Public appearance disclosures
When an analyst makes a public appearance, she must disclose any conflicts or holdings in the stocks she discusses.
A television analyst states that she owns the stock she is recommending.
Disclosures are required only in written reports.
Prohibited compensation
A research analyst must not accept compensation from a subject company that could influence the opinion, and any compensation must be disclosed.

An analyst may accept gifts from the company with no disclosure.
Grievance and penalties
Violations of the regulations can lead to penalties, suspension or cancellation of registration by SEBI.

SEBI has no power to penalise research analysts.
Recommendation requirements
Each recommendation must be supported by research data and a rating system, and reports must carry the required disclaimers and disclosures.

Reports need not carry any disclaimers.
Associate's trading
The trading restrictions and disclosure duties also apply to an analyst's associates and relatives where specified in the regulations.

facts: Dow theory
Dow theory holds that markets move in primary, secondary and minor trends, and that averages must confirm each other.

Trend
A trend is the general direction of price movement: an uptrend has higher highs and higher lows, a downtrend lower highs and lower lows.
A chart shows each peak and trough above the last.
An uptrend has lower highs.
Support
Support is a price level where buying interest is strong enough to stop a decline temporarily.
A stock repeatedly bounces from ₹100.

Resistance
Resistance is a price level where selling pressure tends to halt a rise temporarily.
A stock fails to cross ₹150 several times.

Breakout
A breakout is a price move beyond support or resistance, ideally on higher volume, signalling a possible new trend.
A stock closes above its long-held resistance on heavy volume.

Simple moving average
A simple moving average is the average closing price over a set number of periods, smoothing price data to show the trend.
A 50-day average of closing prices.

Exponential moving average
An exponential moving average gives greater weight to recent prices and reacts faster than a simple average.
An analyst prefers an average that responds more quickly to new prices.
An EMA gives equal weight to all days.
Golden cross
A golden cross occurs when a shorter-term average, such as the 50-day, crosses above a longer-term average, such as the 200-day, a bullish signal.
The 50-day average rises above the 200-day average.
A golden cross is a bearish signal.
Death cross
A death cross occurs when the 50-day average crosses below the 200-day average, a bearish signal.
The shorter average falls beneath the longer one.
A death cross is a bullish signal.
RSI
The Relative Strength Index is a momentum oscillator from 0 to 100; above 70 is considered overbought and below 30 oversold.
A reading of 78 suggests the stock may be overbought.
An RSI above 70 means oversold.
MACD
MACD is the difference between a 12-period and 26-period EMA, with a 9-period signal line; crossovers indicate momentum changes.
A line crossing above its signal line suggests rising momentum.
MACD measures trading volume.
Bollinger Bands
Bollinger Bands plot a moving average with bands two standard deviations above and below, showing volatility and extremes.
Bands widen when volatility rises.
Bollinger Bands show company earnings.
Stochastic oscillator
The stochastic oscillator compares a closing price with the range over a period; above 80 is overbought and below 20 oversold.
A reading of 15 suggests an oversold stock.
A stochastic reading above 80 is oversold.
On-balance volume
On-balance volume adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days, to see whether volume confirms the price trend.
A rising price with falling OBV is a warning sign.
OBV is a measure of earnings.
Volume confirmation
A price move accompanied by rising volume is considered more reliable than one on thin volume.
A rally on heavy volume is trusted more.
Volume is irrelevant to price moves.
Head and shoulders
A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with the middle highest, and signals a potential trend reversal from up to down when the neckline breaks.
A chart shows a left shoulder, higher head and right shoulder.
A head and shoulders pattern signals a continuing uptrend.
Double top
A double top is a bearish reversal pattern in which price makes two peaks at a similar level and then breaks below the trough between them.

A double top is a bullish pattern.
Double bottom
A double bottom is a bullish reversal pattern with two troughs at a similar level followed by a break above the middle peak.
Price falls to ₹80 twice and then rises.
A double bottom is a bearish pattern.
Triangle pattern
Triangles are consolidation patterns where price ranges narrow; ascending triangles often break upward and descending ones downward.
Price makes lower highs and a flat support line.
Triangles show the maximum volatility.
Cup and handle
The cup and handle is a bullish continuation pattern with a rounded bottom followed by a small pullback before a breakout.
A rounded base is followed by a small consolidation and a rise.
A cup and handle is a bearish reversal.
Candlestick
A candlestick shows open, high, low and close for a period, with the body showing the open-to-close range and wicks showing extremes.
A candle has a long lower wick and small body.
A candlestick shows only closing price.
Doji
A doji forms when the open and close are almost equal, signalling indecision between buyers and sellers.
A candle with almost no body and long wicks.
A doji shows a strong trend.
Bullish engulfing
A bullish engulfing pattern is a large up candle that completely covers the previous down candle, suggesting a reversal upwards.
A big green candle swallows the previous red one after a decline.
A bullish engulfing pattern appears at the top of an uptrend.
Fibonacci retracement

A stock falls back to 61.8% of the previous rally and bounces.
Fibonacci levels predict company earnings.
Gap
A gap is an empty space between one day's range and the next, showing sudden change in sentiment, often after news.
A stock opens well above the previous day's high.
A gap means the stock did not trade.
Advance-decline line
The advance-decline line tracks the number of advancing minus declining stocks and shows the breadth of a market move.
The index rises while fewer stocks advance, a sign of narrow breadth.
The advance-decline line measures interest rates.
Open interest in analysis
Rising open interest with rising prices indicates fresh buying and strengthens the trend; falling open interest suggests short covering or unwinding.
Prices and open interest rise together.
Open interest measures a stock's daily volume.
Limitations of technical analysis
Technical signals can fail and give false breakouts; they are best used with risk limits and alongside other analysis.
A breakout reverses within days and stops out traders.
Technical signals are always accurate.
Elliott wave
Elliott wave theory proposes that markets move in repeating waves of five impulse and three corrective moves, although interpretation is subjective.
An analyst labels price moves as waves.
Elliott wave is a precise mathematical law.
Relative strength comparison
Relative strength compares a security's performance with a benchmark or peers to identify leaders and laggards.
An analyst picks stocks outperforming the index.

cases: Alpha Ltd reports revenue of ₹1,200 crore, EBITDA of ₹240 crore, depreciation of ₹60 crore and interest of ₹30 crore. The tax rate is 25%. It has 10 crore shares, shareholders' equity of ₹800 crore and debt of ₹400 crore.
Beta Ltd trades at ₹300. Its EPS is ₹15, book value per share is ₹100 and it pays a dividend of ₹6 per share. The average P/E of its industry is 18.
Gamma Ltd closed at ₹100, ₹102, ₹104, ₹103 and ₹106 over the last five sessions. Its 14-day RSI is now 78. Today it broke above a resistance level of ₹105 on volume twice the average.

Ravi, a registered research analyst, plans to publish a report on Zeta Ltd. He owns shares worth 1.5% of Zeta's equity. Zeta's investment bankers have offered to pay him for the report. He also plans to buy more Zeta shares the day before publication.
X Ltd has a net profit margin of 8%, asset turnover of 1.5 and an equity multiplier of 2. Y Ltd has a net margin of 12%, asset turnover of 0.8 and an equity multiplier of 2.5.

Delta Ltd is expected to generate free cash flow to the firm of ₹100 crore, ₹110 crore and ₹121 crore in the next three years. After year 3 it will grow at 4% a year for ever. The discount rate (WACC) is 12%. Net debt is ₹200 crore and there are 10 crore shares.

The risk-free rate is 7% and the expected market return is 12%. Stock A has a beta of 1.2 and an expected return of 14%. Stock B has a beta of 0.7 and an expected return of 9%. A portfolio holds 60% in A and 40% in B. The portfolio's standard deviation is 15%.
The central bank cuts the repo rate by 50 basis points. Retail inflation has eased to 4%, GDP growth is steady at 6.5% and the rupee is stable. An analyst must update her sector views.

Omega Ltd reports PAT up 25%. But: operating cash flow is negative; receivable days rose from 60 to 110; 60% of the promoters' shares are pledged; related-party sales are 25% of revenue; and the statutory auditor and CFO both resigned within a year.

Sigma Ltd's shares trade at ₹900 with a face value of ₹10 and an EPS of ₹30. The company announces a bonus issue of 1 share for every 2 held, followed by a stock split of ₹10 into ₹2 per share. An investor holds 100 shares.
